t.title: Pruebas a lo largo del ciclo de vida del desarrollo de software

t.e: Evaluating work products is one of the typical objectives (1.1.1). Proving the absence of defects is impossible (principle 1), locating and eliminating the cause is debugging, and exhaustive testing is impossible (principle 2).
Providing information to stakeholders to enable informed decision-making (e.g., the release decision) is a typical objective of testing.
The syllabus states that objectives vary depending on the context: work product under test, test level, risks, life cycle, and business factors (corporate structure, competition, time to market).
Verifying compliance with contractual, legal, and regulatory requirements appears literally among the typical objectives of testing.
Checking that the system meets user expectations in its environment is validation. Verifying specified requirements is verification; both are distinct objectives.
Fixing defects is debugging, an activity that is not testing. The other three options are indeed typical objectives of testing.
Debugging reproduces the failure, diagnoses (finds the defect) and fixes it. Executing, re-executing (confirmation testing) and designing tests are testing.
According to 1.1.2, the typical debugging process is: reproducing the failure, diagnosing (finding the defect) and fixing the defect.
When static testing finds a defect, debugging consists only of removing it: there is no need to reproduce or diagnose, because static testing finds defects directly and does not cause failures.
The syllabus indicates that, preferably, confirmation testing is performed by the same person who performed the initial testing.
Testing and debugging are separate activities: testing causes failures (dynamic) or finds defects (static); debugging seeks causes, analyzes them and removes them.
After confirmation, regression checks that the fix has not caused failures in other parts of the test object.

Testers indirectly represent users, as including a representative group of users is usually expensive and unfeasible. Testing does not eliminate defects (that is debugging) nor does it guarantee the absence of defects.
Testing detects defects cost-effectively; they are then removed through debugging, which is not a testing activity. Therefore, it contributes to quality indirectly.

Testing directly evaluates the quality of the test object in various phases, and these measures support decisions such as phase transition or release. Additionally, any stakeholder can use testing skills.
The syllabus mentions that testing may be mandatory due to contractual, legal, or regulatory requirements.
As quality control, testing helps achieve agreed objectives within scope, time, quality, and budget constraints. Its contribution is not limited to the testing team.
The syllabus explains that the alternative (including representative users) is usually not possible due to high costs and the lack of suitable available users.
Testing: product-oriented, corrective, a form of quality control. QA: process-oriented, preventive, everyone's responsibility in the project.
The syllabus states that QA applies to development and testing processes and is everyone's responsibility in the project.
In testing, results are used to correct defects; in QA, they provide feedback on the performance of development and testing processes.
The syllabus cites formal methods (model checking and correctness proofs), simulation, and prototyping as other forms of quality control.
QA is based on the premise that a good process followed correctly produces a good product; therefore, it focuses on implementing and improving processes.
According to 1.2.2, testing is a primary form of quality control. QA is preventive, process-oriented, and applies to both development and testing.

Error (mistake) → defect → failure. The misunderstanding is the error, the incorrect calculation in the code is the defect, and the observed incorrect total is the failure. Time pressure would be a possible root cause.

The syllabus indicates that some defects always cause failures when executed, others only under specific circumstances, and others never. Additionally, defects in early products often cause defects in later products.
Failures can also be caused by environmental conditions, such as radiation or electromagnetic fields that cause defects in the firmware.
The root cause is the fundamental reason for a problem (e.g., the situation leading to an error). It is identified through root cause analysis, and addressing it helps prevent similar defects.
Lack of training is a fundamental reason leading to human errors: a root cause. Correcting it can prevent similar defects or reduce their frequency.
Defects can be in documentation (a requirements specification, a test script), in source code, or in supporting work products such as a build file.
"Tests wear out": Repeating the same tests makes them less effective at finding new defects; they need to be modified or new tests created.
The fallacy of the absence of defects: verifying all requirements and correcting all defects does not guarantee that the system satisfies users. In addition to verification, validation is required.

"Testing shows the presence, not the absence of defects": even if no defects are found, testing cannot demonstrate that the test object is correct; it only reduces the probability that defects remain.
Since testing everything is not feasible except in trivial cases, the syllabus recommends techniques, prioritization, and risk-based testing to focus effort.
Defect clustering: a small number of components contain the majority of defects (Pareto principle). Expected and observed clusters feed into risk-based testing.
There is no universal testing approach: testing is done differently in different contexts.
Defects removed early do not cause derived defects and reduce the cost of quality; therefore, it is advisable to start early with static and dynamic testing.
The syllabus indicates that, in some cases, repeating the same tests is beneficial, for example in automated regression testing.
Principle 4 (defects cluster) explicitly mentions that clusters of defects, both expected and observed, are an important input for risk-based testing.
10^12 combinations cannot be tested: exhaustive testing is impossible except in trivial cases. Techniques and prioritization must be used.
Analysis answers "what to test": the test basis is analyzed and test conditions are defined and prioritized. Design answers "how to test".

Closure occurs at milestones (release, end of iteration...): useful testware is archived, lessons learned are collected, the environment is left in an agreed state, and the completion report is written.
Design ("how to test") converts conditions into test cases and other testware (e.g., test charters), identifies coverage items, and defines data and environment requirements.

In implementation, the necessary testware for execution (data) is created or acquired, procedures are organized into suites, scripts are created, the execution schedule is prepared, and the environment is built and verified.
Monitoring compares actual progress with the plan; control takes the necessary actions to meet test objectives.
The syllabus indicates that, although they may seem to follow a logical sequence, activities are usually performed iteratively or in parallel and must be adapted to the system and the project.
Context factors: stakeholders, team members, business domain, technical factors, project constraints, organizational factors, the lifecycle, and tools.
Context factors affect the strategy, techniques, degree of automation, required coverage, level of detail of testware, and reporting.
The syllabus lists "Team members (skills, knowledge, level of experience, availability, training needs)" as a context-specific factor.
Scope, time, budget, and resources are project constraints.
Testing is not done in isolation: it is part of the organization's development processes and is funded by stakeholders to meet their business needs.
Software type, product architecture, and technology used are technical factors.
Implementation products: procedures, manual and automated scripts, suites, data, execution schedule, and environment elements (stubs, drivers, simulators, service virtualization).
Analysis produces test conditions (prioritized), such as acceptance criteria, and defect reports from the test basis. Test charters are from design; logs are from execution.
The syllabus cites them as examples of test environment items, which are products of test implementation.
Execution produces test logs and defect reports.
All of them are products of test design ("how to test").
Planning products: test plan, schedule, risk register, and entry and exit criteria. Progress reports are from test monitoring and control.
Traceability allows evaluating coverage, determining the impact of changes, facilitates audits, and helps meet IT governance criteria.
The syllabus gives this example: tracing results to risks allows evaluating the residual risk of the test object.
Tracing test cases to requirements allows verifying that requirements are covered.
Including the status of test basis items makes reports more understandable and helps communicate technical aspects to stakeholders.
Accurate traceability supports coverage assessment; measurable coverage criteria can function as KPIs indicating the extent to which objectives are met.
Good traceability facilitates audits, helps meet IT governance criteria, and provides information on product quality, process capability, and project progress.
The test management role assumes overall responsibility for the process and focuses on planning, monitoring, control, and closure.
The testing role assumes responsibility for the engineering (technical) aspect of testing: analysis, design, implementation, and execution.
The syllabus indicates that different people can assume the roles at different times, and that the same person can have both at the same time.
In agile, part of the test management tasks are assumed by the team; those that span multiple teams or the entire organization can be performed by test managers external to the team.
The syllabus gives as examples of who can perform the management role: a team leader, a test manager, or a development lead.
Designing test cases is an engineering task (testing role). Planning, controlling, and closing correspond to the management role.
Testers often bring bad news, and communicating results can be perceived as criticism. Confirmation bias makes it hard to accept contrary information; defects must be communicated constructively.
The syllabus associates technical knowledge with efficiency (e.g., using appropriate tools). Testing knowledge, analytical thinking, and creativity increase effectiveness.
Domain knowledge enables understanding end users and business stakeholders and communicating with them.
According to 1.5.1, being thorough, careful, curious, methodical, and attentive to detail helps in finding defects, especially those that are difficult to detect.
To improve the perception of testing as a destructive activity, information about defects and failures must be communicated constructively.
The syllabus mentions confirmation bias: it can make it difficult to accept information that contradicts what one believes.
In the whole-team approach, anyone with the necessary knowledge can perform any task, and everyone is responsible for quality.
The syllabus indicates that the whole-team approach originates from Extreme Programming.
Advantages: improves team dynamics, communication, and collaboration, and creates synergy by leveraging diverse skills.
Testers help business representatives create appropriate acceptance tests, and agree with developers on the test strategy and automation.
The syllabus states that in contexts such as safety-critical systems, a high level of test independence may be required, so the whole-team approach may not be suitable.
Sharing space (physical or virtual) facilitates communication and interaction.
With developers, testers agree on the test strategy and decide on automation approaches; thus transferring testing knowledge to the team.
Key to the whole-team approach: everyone is responsible for quality.
By working closely with the team, testers transfer testing knowledge and influence product development.
The syllabus states that the whole team approach is supported by the ability to work effectively in a team and contribute to its objectives.
Disadvantages: team isolation, communication problems or adversarial relationship, developers losing a sense of responsibility for quality, and testers seen as a bottleneck.
Author: no independence. Same team colleagues: some. Testers outside the team within the organization: high. Testers external to the organization: very high.
The main advantage is that, due to their different knowledge, perspectives, and biases, independent testers detect different types of defects than developers.
The syllabus recommends several levels of independence: developers in component and component integration, the test team in system and system integration, and business in acceptance.
Independence does not replace familiarity: developers can efficiently find many defects in their own code.
Testers from outside the organization = very high independence.

t.sum: Testing is a set of activities to discover defects and assess the quality of work products (test objects). It is not just execution: it also includes static activities, planning, management… and combines verification (does it meet specifications?) with validation (does it cover real needs?). Typical objectives: assess work products, provoke failures and find defects, ensure coverage, reduce risk, verify requirements and legal compliance, report to stakeholders to decide, generate confidence, and validate. Objectives change depending on the context.

Testing and debugging are distinct activities. Dynamic testing causes failures; static testing finds defects directly. Debugging seeks the cause (the defect), analyzes it, and eliminates it: reproduce → diagnose → correct. This is followed by confirmation testing (preferably performed by the person who conducted the initial testing) and regression testing. If the defect was found by static testing, it is sufficient to eliminate it.

Testing is a cost-effective way to detect defects, which are then eliminated through debugging: it contributes to quality indirectly. It measures quality at each phase and supports decisions (such as release), indirectly represents users (involving them directly is usually expensive), and may be mandatory by contract, law, or regulation.

Testing ≠ QA. Testing is product-oriented and corrective: it is a form of quality control, as are formal methods, simulation, or prototyping. QA is process-oriented and preventive (a good process yields a good product), and is everyone's responsibility. Test results serve testing to correct defects and serve QA as feedback on processes.

A person commits an error (mistake) that introduces a defect (bug, fault) into a work product; if the defect is executed, it may produce a failure. Not every defect always produces a failure, and some failures are due to the environment (radiation, electromagnetic fields). The root cause is the fundamental reason for the problem; addressing it prevents similar defects.

1) Testing shows the presence of defects, not their absence. 2) Exhaustive testing is impossible: techniques, prioritization, and risks must be used. 3) Testing early saves time and money. 4) Defects cluster (Pareto), which feeds risk-based testing. 5) Tests wear out: repeating them makes them ineffective at finding new defects, except in automated regression. 6) Testing is context-dependent. 7) Fallacy of absence of defects: verification is not enough; validation is also required.

Planning (objectives and approach) · Monitoring and control (compare with the plan and correct) · Analysis ("what to test": prioritized conditions derived from the test basis) · Design ("how to test": cases, test charters, coverage items, data and environment requirements) · Implementation (procedures, scripts, suites, data, execution schedule, ready environment) · Execution (execute, compare, record, analyze anomalies) · Closure (archive testware, completion report, lessons learned). These are usually performed iteratively or in parallel.

The way of testing depends on the context: stakeholders, team, business domain (criticality, risks, regulations), technical factors, project constraints (scope, time, budget), organization, lifecycle, and tools. This affects the strategy, techniques, automation, coverage, detail of testware, and reporting.

Each activity produces testware. Planning: plan, schedule, risk register, entry and exit criteria. Monitoring and control: progress reports, control directives. Analysis: prioritized conditions (e.g., acceptance criteria) and defect reports from the test basis. Design: cases, test charters, coverage items, data and environment requirements. Implementation: procedures, scripts, suites, data, execution schedule, stubs, drivers, simulators. Execution: logs and defect reports. Closure: completion report, lessons learned, change requests.

Maintaining traceability between test basis, testware, results, and defects allows evaluating coverage (requirements covered, residual risk), analyzing the impact of changes, facilitating audits and IT governance, and producing understandable reports that show the status of each element of the test basis.

There are two main roles. Test management: responsible for the process and the team; focuses on planning, monitoring, control, and closure. Testing: responsible for the technical aspect; focuses on analysis, design, implementation, and execution. One person can have both roles; in agile, part of the management is assumed by the team.

Key skills: testing knowledge (effectiveness), thoroughness and curiosity (finding difficult defects), communication and active listening, analytical and critical thinking and creativity, technical knowledge (efficiency) and domain knowledge (speaking with users). Since the tester often delivers bad news, they must communicate defects constructively, taking into account confirmation bias.

It comes from Extreme Programming: anyone with the necessary skill can perform any task, and everyone is responsible for quality. They share the space (physical or virtual). Advantages: better dynamics, communication, and collaboration, and synergy. Testers help the business with acceptance testing and agree with development on strategy and automation. It may not fit critical systems that require high independence.

Levels: author (none), team peers (some), testers from outside the team but within the organization (high), external testers (very high). It is usually ideal to combine several levels. Advantages: they detect other types of defects and question assumptions. Disadvantages: isolation, communication issues, developers lose responsibility for quality, and testers are seen as a bottleneck.

t.q: ¿Cuál de los siguientes es un objetivo de prueba típico?

o: Los objetivos de prueba pueden variar según el contexto, como el nivel de prueba, los riesgos y el ciclo de vida del software (SDLC) que se esté siguiendo
Los objetivos de prueba son los mismos para todos los proyectos y todos los niveles de prueba

Los objetivos de prueba se definen únicamente después de finalizar la ejecución de la prueba

t.q: ¿Qué actividad forma parte de la depuración en lugar de la prueba?

o: Reproducir el fallo, diagnosticar (encontrar el defecto), corregir el defecto
Corregir el defecto, reproducir el fallo, informar del defecto

El defecto debe ser confirmado por la prueba dinámica antes de poder ser eliminado

o: La prueba puede provocar fallos o encontrar directamente defectos; la depuración encuentra, analiza y elimina las causas de los fallos
La prueba elimina defectos; la depuración los encuentra

Para reproducir el fallo original una vez más
Para diagnosticar la causa raíz del defecto original
